label: From integrated to infinitesimal
notes: This chapter, printed pages 525 to 544, sharpens displacement convexity from a chord inequality along the whole geodesic into a pointwise second-derivative criterion. We motivate why a local Bochner-type identity is exactly equivalent to the integrated K-convexity bound, and preview the curvature-weighted integral that will carry the argument forward.

label: Displacement convexity recalled
notes: We recall that a functional is K-displacement convex when its values along every Wasserstein geodesic lie below the K-modified chord. The chord form is global; our task this chapter is to differentiate twice in time and read off the equivalent infinitesimal statement that holds at each moment of the path.

label: The entropy along a geodesic
notes: Boltzmann entropy is the model functional. Along a displacement interpolation driven by a Kantorovich potential, the density evolves by a continuity equation. We set up the time-dependent density and velocity field so that the first and second time derivatives of entropy become tractable transport integrals over the moving measure.

label: First derivative: the velocity field
notes: Differentiating entropy once produces an integral pairing the density's evolution against the logarithmic gradient. We identify the velocity field as the gradient of the potential and rewrite the first derivative as a divergence integral, the clean starting point from which a second differentiation will expose the curvature term.

label: Second derivative and Bochner
notes: The heart of the chapter: differentiating a second time and integrating by parts yields the Bochner formula. The commutator of gradient and Laplacian along the flow splits the result into the squared Hessian of the potential plus a Ricci quadratic form acting on its gradient, the curvature signature we seek.

label: The curvature-weighted integral
notes: Collecting terms, the second derivative of entropy equals the integral over the moving measure of the Hessian energy plus the Ricci form evaluated on the velocity. Every contribution is weighted by the density, so the identity is genuinely a curvature-weighted average rather than a single pointwise number at one place.

label: Two nonnegative pieces
notes: We dissect the integrand into a manifestly nonnegative dissipation term, the squared Frobenius norm of the Hessian, and a curvature term carrying the Ricci tensor's sign. Under a Ricci lower bound the second piece is controlled, and the whole second derivative is bounded below by the curvature constant times kinetic energy.

label: Fisher information appears
notes: The Hessian energy is intimately tied to the Fisher information of the evolving density. We show how the dissipation term, when the velocity is a logarithmic gradient, reproduces the Fisher information functional, explaining why entropy dissipation and Fisher information are the two faces of the same second-order object.

label: Local equals integrated
notes: We prove the equivalence: the pointwise lower bound on the second derivative integrates to the K-convexity chord inequality, and conversely the chord bound forces the infinitesimal inequality at almost every time. This two-way passage is the chapter's organizing principle, mirroring the Gamma-two calculus of Bakry and Emery.

label: CD(K,N) and the dimensional term
notes: Refining the bound, we incorporate the dimension N by isolating the trace of the Hessian and applying Cauchy-Schwarz. This yields the dimensional curvature-dimension inequality, where a Bochner remainder of the squared Laplacian divided by N tightens the pure Ricci estimate into the sharp CD(K,N) condition.

label: Numerical residual check
notes: To make the abstract identity inspectable, we evaluate a toy second-variation residual on a two-dimensional grid. Adding the chosen Ricci lower-bound term renders the residual nonnegative everywhere; lowering the curvature constant past a threshold produces the first negative cells, exactly the failure the theorem predicts and warns about.

label: Synthesis and outlook
notes: We close by tying the infinitesimal criterion to its uses: gradient flows, functional inequalities, and the synthetic definition of Ricci bounds on metric measure spaces. The curvature-weighted second derivative is the bridge from smooth Riemannian Bochner calculus to the nonsmooth Lott-Sturm-Villani theory developed in the chapters that follow.
